what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat serious bacterial infections in adults, including infections in the abdomen (belly area) and urinary tract (bladder and kidneys). It works by killing certain bacteria that are hard to treat with other antibiotics. A doctor will decide if this antibiotic is right for your type of infection.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic setting. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home. Each dose is given slowly over about 3 hours. It is very important to receive every scheduled dose for the full length of time your doctor prescribed, even if you start feeling better sooner.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 500 mg of aztreonam and 167 mg of avibactam (one full dose) given every 8 hours (3 times a day) through your IV. Each infusion takes about 3 hours to complete. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have kidney problems. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, a missed dose is unlikely. However, if you miss or are late for a scheduled infusion, tell your nurse or doctor right away. They will decide the best time to give your next dose. Do not try to 'double up' or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: You will not need to store this medicine at home since it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. In the medical setting, the prepared IV solution should be kept refrigerated and used within the time frame recommended by the pharmacist. Unused portions of the mixed solution should be safely discarded by medical staff.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this antibiotic. Avoid taking probenecid (a gout medicine) while receiving this medicine, as it can change how your body processes this antibiotic. Do not stop treatment early, even if you feel better, as this can allow the infection to come back and become harder to treat.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or nurse right away if you experience any of the following: signs of an allergic reaction such as skin rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing; severe diarrhea or stomach cramps that are watery or bloody (this could be a sign of a serious bowel infection called C. difficile); signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark-colored urine, or severe stomach pain; seizures; or any unusual or worsening symptoms during or after your treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting treatment, but it is very important to complete the full course your doctor prescribed. Lab tests and your doctor's evaluation will help confirm that the infection is clearing up. Do not stop treatment early just because you feel better.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. If your kidneys are not working well, your dose will be lowered to prevent side effects. Liver problems: Use with caution if you have liver disease; your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before receiving this medicine, as the safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not fully established and your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits carefully. Elderly patients: Older adults are more likely to have kidney problems, so dose adjustments may be needed. Children: This medicine has not been approved for use in patients under 18 years of age.
